title: Email overload: exploring personal information management of email
abstract: Field observations showed that email had expanded beyond communication into task management and personal archiving. Users kept messages representing outstanding tasks, partially processed documents, and ongoing conversations in their inboxes, creating overload and making important work difficult to track.

title: E-mail as habitat: an exploration of embedded personal information management
abstract: The study characterizes email as a work habitat used for information management, coordination, and collaboration rather than merely communication. Substantial amounts of organizational work are received and delegated through email, making it central to personal work management.

title: Taking Email to Task: The Design and Evaluation of a Task Management Centered Email Tool
abstract: Taskmaster redesigns an email client around task management, embedding task-centric resources and representations in the email interface. Studies using participants' live email over two weeks found benefits from organizing messages around work tasks rather than treating each message independently.

title: What a to-do: studies of task management towards the design of a personal task list manager
abstract: The authors studied the media people use to record and organize to-dos and followed how tasks are completed over time. They found that users employ sophisticated prioritization strategies and identified factors influencing task completion and the usefulness of different task representations.

title: Learning to Classify Email into “Speech Acts”
abstract: The paper learns to classify email by sender intent using categories such as propose, commit, deliver, meeting, information, and task. The motivating applications include tracking ongoing joint activities, commitments, requests, deadlines, delegated subtasks, and reminders from ordinary unstructured email.

title: On the collective classification of email "speech acts"
abstract: The paper classifies email messages for acts such as requests and commitments while exploiting sequential correlations among messages in the same thread. A dependency-network collective classifier improves classification for some email-act categories over a bag-of-words baseline.

title: A hybrid learning system for recognizing user tasks from desktop activities and email messages
abstract: The TaskTracer system associates user-defined work activities with files, folders, email messages, contacts, and web pages accessed while performing them. The paper develops machine-learning methods for recognizing the user's current task from activity traces spanning desktop resources and email.

title: eAssistant: Cognitive Assistance for Identification and Auto-Triage of Actionable Conversations
abstract: eAssistant identifies actionable information such as requests and promises across productivity applications including email, chat, messaging, and enterprise collaboration tools. Its action-identification model is personalizable, online-trainable, and continuously updated from user interactions and feedback, and it uses user-centric conversation characteristics for auto-triage.

title: RemindMe: Plugging a Reminder Manager into Email for Enhancing Workplace Responsiveness
abstract: RemindMe integrates reminder management with workplace email to reduce the cognitive overhead of handling incoming and outgoing requests. The system targets the common workplace problem of remembering follow-ups and maintaining responsiveness to colleagues.

title: The Learning Behind Gmail Priority Inbox
abstract: Priority Inbox learns a separate statistical importance model for each user and ranks mail by the probability that the user will act on it. The models are updated frequently from user behavior, making the work a large-scale example of near-online personalized learning under noisy and changing interaction data.
venue: NIPS 2010 Workshop on Learning on Cores, Clusters and Clouds

title: Attention-Sensitive Alerting
abstract: The paper develops utility-directed alerting methods that balance the cost of delaying information against the cost of interrupting a user under uncertainty. Its email case study models expected message criticality and uses that estimate to prioritize messages and decide how notifications should be delivered.

title: Prospective memory: when reminders fail
abstract: Four experiments tested whether reminders necessarily improve prospective memory. Reminders specifying both the triggering event and the intended action were most effective, while target-only reminders could perform no better than receiving no reminder, showing that reminder value depends on what information is resurfaced.

title: How important is importance for prospective memory? A review
abstract: This review examines how the perceived importance of an intention affects prospective-memory performance. It synthesizes evidence involving rewards, relative and absolute importance, social motives, cognitive load, task type, and motivation, providing a basis for reasoning about reminder value beyond recency alone.

title: Overview of the TAC 2008 Update Summarization Task
abstract: TAC 2008 required systems to generate an initial summary and then an update summary for a later related document set under the assumption that the reader had already consumed the earlier material. Systems were assessed using automatic metrics and manual judgments of content, readability, and overall responsiveness.

title: Squibs: Nouveau-ROUGE: A Novelty Metric for Update Summarization
abstract: The paper argues that conventional ROUGE does not adequately evaluate update summaries because it does not explicitly penalize information already conveyed to the reader. Nouveau-ROUGE measures both similarity to update reference summaries and redundancy with earlier summaries, targeting novelty and repetition together.

title: A New Approach for Multi-Document Update Summarization
abstract: The method formulates an update summary as information about a current document cluster conditioned on a prior cluster that the reader has already seen. It evaluates the resulting summaries on DUC and TAC 2007–2009 data using human summaries and ROUGE.
venue: Journal of Computer Science and Technology

title: Taking into account Inter-sentence Similarity for Update Summarization
abstract: The paper extends coverage-and-length optimization for extractive update summarization by explicitly incorporating semantic sentence similarity to control redundancy. It evaluates the approach on DUC 2007 and TAC 2008 and 2009 update-summarization datasets.

title: Updating Users about Time Critical Events
abstract: The work studies how to select novel and important information from a continuing news stream as an event develops. It combines information-retrieval and multi-document-summarization techniques and proposes an evaluation approach for time-critical user updates.

title: TREC 2013 Temporal Summarization
abstract: The TREC track evaluates online systems that monitor developing events and emit short, relevant, reliable, and timely updates while avoiding redundant information. It also explicitly considers tracking the changing values of important event attributes and evaluates gain, comprehensiveness, and latency-related properties.

title: HLTCOE at TREC 2013: Temporal Summarization
abstract: The system addresses sequential update summarization by processing a temporally ordered stream and selecting sentences containing relevant, new, and important information. Unlike earlier batch update-summarization settings, the TREC task requires continuous and immediate updates.

title: A Multi-level System for Sequential Update Summarization
abstract: The paper develops a multi-level system that combines topic-level and sentence-level analysis to produce useful, new, and timely updates about developing events. It evaluates the approach using the TREC Temporal Summarization sequential-update task.

title: Mining Sequential Update Summarization with Hierarchical Text Analysis
abstract: The paper formalizes sequential update summarization and develops a hierarchical topic- and sentence-level update-mining system. Evaluation on TREC 2013 uses expected gain, expected latency gain, comprehensiveness, and latency comprehensiveness, exposing precision/recall and timeliness tradeoffs for repeated updates.

title: From Moments to Milestones: Incremental Timeline Summarization Leveraging Large Language Models
abstract: The approach constructs event and topic timelines from a text stream using incremental event clustering, with large language models serving as pseudo-oracles for event detection. It is evaluated across four timeline-summarization benchmarks and provides a transferable mechanism for maintaining evolving event identity over incoming information.

title: Corpus-Based Problem Selection for EHR Note Summarization
abstract: As a step toward longitudinal patient-history summarization, the paper studies automatic selection of patient problems from accumulated clinical notes. Its focus on identifying problems that remain relevant to the current state provides a transferable model for retaining persistent items from long histories.

title: HARVEST, a longitudinal patient record summarizer
abstract: HARVEST is a problem-based interactive temporal summarizer and visualization for longitudinal patient records. It aggregates information around clinically meaningful problems across time and care settings and was evaluated in point-of-care review tasks, making it relevant to persistent work-item identity and state tracking.
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

title: Reducing Physicians' Cognitive Load During Chart Review: A Problem-Oriented Summary of the Patient Electronic Record
abstract: ProSPER organizes longitudinal electronic health-record information around an automatically generated problem list and disease-specific views. Developed from 1,500 longitudinal patient records, it combines multiple NLP components to provide comprehensive problem-oriented summaries intended to reduce review burden.

title: Large Language Models with Temporal Reasoning for Longitudinal Clinical Summarization and Prediction
abstract: The study evaluates open-source LLMs, retrieval-augmented variants, and chain-of-thought prompting on long patient trajectories containing structured and unstructured data spread across time. It specifically tests temporal coherence in longitudinal summarization and prediction and finds continuing difficulty with temporal progression.

title: CLIN-SUMM: Incremental Longitudinal Summarization of Clinical Notes Enables Scalable Representation and Early Disease Prediction
abstract: CLIN-SUMM treats summarization as an incremental longitudinal representation problem rather than repeatedly collapsing the entire history into a static summary. It constructs structured, date-partitioned representations encounter by encounter using only information available at that time, and evaluates correctness and completeness as well as downstream longitudinal prediction.

title: Cross-Document Event Coreference: Annotations, Experiments, and Observations
abstract: This foundational work studies how mentions of the same event can be identified across document boundaries, with annotations and experiments on cross-document event coreference. The task provides a transferable mechanism for maintaining stable semantic identity when information about one matter is distributed across multiple sources.

title: Generalizing Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution Across Multiple Corpora
abstract: The paper evaluates cross-document event-coreference systems across several corpora rather than within a single dataset. It finds substantial domain-dependent behavior and overfitting, and argues that broadly applicable multi-document identity resolution requires multi-corpus evaluation.

title: Cross-document Event Identity via Dense Annotation
abstract: The paper develops dense annotations for deciding event identity across related documents instead of restricting annotations to a small set of event types. It also records overlapping contextual dimensions including time, location, and participants, and explicitly considers quasi-identity between related events.

title: Cross-document Event Coreference Search: Task, Dataset and Modeling
abstract: Given an event mention as a query, this task requires finding all coreferring mentions in a large document collection. The paper introduces a dataset and retrieval-based models, providing a mechanism for collecting dispersed evidence referring to the same event across source boundaries.

title: Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution on Discourse Structure
abstract: The paper clusters event mentions across multiple documents that refer to the same real-world event. It augments local mention similarity with global discourse structure to capture interactions between distant event mentions, improving cross-document coreference resolution on ECB+.

title: Synergetic Event Understanding: A Collaborative Approach to Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution with Large Language Models
abstract: The work addresses cross-document event coreference by combining large-language-model event understanding with smaller-model representations. Its goal is to cluster mentions from different documents that refer to the same real-world event, providing a modern mechanism for reconciling cross-source event identity.

title: Dynamic user profiles for web personalisation
abstract: The paper develops user profiles that adapt as behavior changes rather than remaining static. It separately models short- and long-term interests and continuously updates the profile from ongoing activity, with evaluation in personalized search.

title: A novel temporal recommender system based on multiple transitions in user preference drift and topic review evolution
abstract: The model explicitly tracks temporal user-preference drift using transitions between time periods, a forgetting-time function, and evolving review topics. Experiments on eight datasets evaluate whether modeling preference change improves recommendations relative to static alternatives.

title: A case study of batch and incremental recommender systems in supermarket data under concept drifts and cold start
abstract: The study compares batch and streaming recommender systems on real data exhibiting changing user preferences and cold-start conditions. Incremental models recover more effectively under concept drift, offering transferable evidence for personalization systems that must adapt to non-stationary users.

title: Constructive Preference Elicitation
abstract: The paper studies interactive learning of user preferences in decision spaces where feasible outcomes are delimited by explicit hard requirements. Preference learning operates over the feasible space while constrained optimization preserves non-negotiable requirements, offering a mechanism for separating hard user rules from softer learned preferences.

title: Learning Modulo Theories for constructive preference elicitation
abstract: CLEO performs interactive preference elicitation for complex configurable objects with both discrete and continuous attributes subject to explicit feasibility constraints. It combines preference learning with constrained optimization rather than treating hard requirements as ordinary weighted features.

title: Interactive Multi-Objective Probabilistic Preference Learning with Soft and Hard Bounds
abstract: The framework distinguishes aspirational soft bounds from non-negotiable hard bounds in interactive multi-objective preference learning. It probabilistically learns user preferences while respecting the different semantics of these two constraint classes, providing a transferable model for precedence between hard rules and softer priorities.

title: Uncertainty Visualizations: Helping Decision Makers Become More Aware of Uncertainty and Its Implications
abstract: The authors develop and evaluate a domain-independent decision-support system that visualizes uncertainty when available information is insufficient to distinguish alternatives. The interface highlights ambiguity and identifies additional information that could reduce it, directly linking uncertainty presentation to information seeking and decision support.
venue: Journal of Cognitive Engineering and Decision Making

title: Communicating uncertainty about facts, numbers and science
abstract: This interdisciplinary review develops a framework for communicating epistemic uncertainty about factual and quantitative claims. It synthesizes evidence on how uncertainty communication can affect cognition, affect, trust, behavior, and decisions, and distinguishes multiple sources and forms of uncertainty.

title: Can You Verifi This? Studying Uncertainty and Decision-Making About Misinformation Using Visual Analytics
abstract: Controlled experiments use a visual-analytics system to study decisions when users encounter uncertain and conflicting information from multiple sources. The presence of conflicting cues systematically changes veracity judgments, providing evidence relevant to presenting disputed information rather than hiding disagreement.

title: How Do Viewers Synthesize Conflicting Information from Data Visualizations?
abstract: Across four experiments, participants integrated sequentially presented visual evidence whose findings could agree or conflict. The study characterizes systematic biases in how people combine contradictory evidence from multiple sources and derives implications for presenting evolving, conflicting information to decision makers.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

title: Strategy-Specific Decision Making with Incomplete Information
abstract: The study tests decision making when the available evidence is incomplete and varies both the amount and structure of information shown to participants. Across several decision strategies, information completeness and presentation structure significantly affect decision performance, offering transferable evidence for briefing interfaces that must expose insufficiently investigated state.
venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
